Tippett-minimum Fusion of Representation-space Diffusion Models for Multi-Encoder Out-of-Distribution Detection

Neelkamal Bhuyan Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology Email: nbhuyan3@gatech.edu
Abstract

We address out-of-distribution (OOD) detection across the full spectrum of distribution shifts—global domain changes, semantic divergence, texture differences, and covariate corruptions—through a multi-encoder fusion of per-encoder representation-space diffusion models (RDMs). We statistically identify each encoder’s sensitivity to specific shift types from ID data alone and introduce EncMin2L—an encoder-agnostic two-level min⁡(⋅)\min(\cdot)-gate that combines and calibrates per-encoder diffusion-based likelihood detectors without OOD labels, outperforming monolithic multi-encoder baselines at ×2.3\!\times lower parameter cost. Two ID-data diagnostics: η2\eta^{2} (class-conditional F-test) and Δ​μ\Delta\mu (log-likelihood shift under synthetic corruptions)—quantify encoder specialization, while a Tippett minimum pp-value combination aggregates per-encoder scores into a single, calibration-stable OOD signal. EncMin2L achieves ≥0.94\geq\!0.94 AUROC across all four shift types simultaneously, outperforming the state-of-the-art representation-space diffusion OOD detectors across overlapping benchmarks.

1 Introduction

Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection asks whether a given image was generated by the same process as the true data, often known as the in-distribution (ID) data. A standard approach fits a density model to ID training data and flags a test point as OOD when its log-likelihood log⁡pθ​(z)\log p_{\theta}(z) falls below a threshold calibrated on held-out ID samples (Xiao et al., 2020). The challenge lies in building density models expressive enough to capture the full structure of the ID distribution yet sensitive to the specific forms of shift that arise in practice.

Deep generative models have become the dominant framework for learning complex data distributions, with diffusion models demonstrating remarkable fidelity across image generation, density estimation, and downstream tasks including anomaly detection and domain adaptation Ho et al. (2020); Livernoche et al. (2024). Score-matching stochastic differential equations (SDEs) (Song et al., 2021b) provide a principled framework: a neural network learns the score function ∇z​log​p​(z)\nabla_{z}\log p(z) via a denoising objective, and the associated probability flow ODE (PF-ODE) enables numerically accurate computation of log⁡pθ​(z)\log p_{\theta}(z) for any test point Song et al. (2021a). This makes score-based diffusion models natural candidates for likelihood-based OOD detection.

Operating diffusion models directly in pixel space is computationally expensive, and pixel-space density estimates are notoriously unreliable for OOD (Xiao et al., 2020; Graham et al., 2023). Representation-space diffusion models (RDMs) address this by operating in the compressed representation space of a pretrained encoder—capturing underlying semantic structure by removing pixel-level variation Rombach et al. (2022). Modern self-supervised encoders are each capable of meaningfully compressing ×224224\!\times\!224 images into dense semantic vectors: CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) encodes global visual-linguistic alignment; DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) captures fine-grained patch-level semantics; and ResNet-50 (He et al., 2016) penultimate features encode texture and low-level image statistics.

This compression is not lossless—each encoder emphasises a different aspect of image structure and is therefore sensitive to a different class of distribution shift. In §4 we quantify this directly: CLIP detects global domain shift but is nearly blind to covariate corruptions; DINOv2 separates fine-grained semantic classes but its features are largely invariant to image corruptions; ResNet-50 is the strongest covariate-shift detector but ranks last on semantic benchmarks. This raises a fundamental question:

Given a library of pretrained encoders, which subset should be deployed, and how should their signals be combined, when the type of distribution shift is unknown at test time?

Main Contributions: We make two contributions that together answer this question. (i) Quantifying encoder sensitivity from ID data. We quantify each encoder’s OOD sensitivity through ID-data diagnostics (η2\eta^{2}, Δ​μ\Delta\mu, and cross-encoder Spearman ρ\rho) and characterise how representation space geometry governs sensitivity to covariate versus semantic distribution shifts. These diagnostics, computed entirely from ID training data, reveal strict encoder specialisation: no encoder dominates across all shift types simultaneously, and any fixed weighting of encoder contributions will underperform on at least one shift type. (ii) Two-level min⁡(⋅)\min(\cdot)-gate with statistical calibration. We combine per-encoder VP-SDE density models through a two-level min⁡(⋅)\min(\cdot)-gate grounded in Tippett’s minimum pp-value test, resulting in our EncMin2L framework. At each level, raw log-likelihood scores are first mapped through the ID empirical CDF to yield calibrated pp-values on [0,1][0,1]. For every encoder, a min⁡(⋅)\min(\cdot) operation across nn different input-normalization forks collapses nn complementary views of each encoder’s representation space into a single per-encoder score (Level 1), followed by an explicit CDF-based re-scaling that corrects for the non-uniform Beta(1,n)(1,n) null distribution of the resulting minimization operation. A second Tippett minimization across all encoders’ Level 1 scores, with a joint threshold τ\tau calibrated on held-out ID data, constitutes the final OOD decision (Level 2). The result is a statistically valid multiple testing procedure in which the input sample itself forces the most-alarmed representation-space diffusion OOD detector to make a decision—adapting to the input without requiring any knowledge of the distribution shift at test time.

We evaluate on four OOD benchmarks spanning global domain shift (SVHN), fine-grained semantic shift (CIFAR-100), texture shift (DTD), and covariate shift (CIFAR-10C). EncMin2L achieves ≥\geq0.94 AUROC across all four benchmarks, outperforming monolithic multi-encoder baselines at 2.3×\times lower parameter cost. Leave-one-out ablations confirm that each encoder specialises on the shift type predicted by its ID diagnostic profile, providing post-hoc validation of the framework.

2 Related Work

Density-based OOD detection.

Using a generative model’s log-likelihood as an OOD score is a longstanding approach. Grathwohl et al. (2020) reformulate a classifier as an energy-based model; Xiao et al. (2020) propose likelihood regret for VAEs to correct for the pathological behaviour of deep generative model likelihoods on OOD inputs. Graham et al. (2023) apply diffusion models directly in pixel space via multi-step reconstruction error; Liu et al. (2023) score checkerboard-masked inpainting with LPIPS (LMD); Heng et al. (2024) extract a compact 6-dimensional descriptor from the denoising trajectory of a pixel-space DM (DiffPath), demonstrating zero-shot cross-distribution generalization but at the cost of coarse OOD resolution. Our work instead trains density models in the compressed representation space of pretrained encoders, where the density is better-behaved and computationally tractable. Järve et al. (2025) independently pursue this direction: their Variational Diffusion Model (VDM) trains a learnable-schedule representation-space diffusion model on a single ResNet-18 encoder and achieves strong AUROC on CIFAR-10 ID benchmarks. Concurrently, Ding et al. (2025) train a sub-VP SDE score model on a single pretrained encoder’s representation space at ImageNet scale, with a class-conditioned variant (ConRDM) that matches supervised detectors when labels are available. Score-based SDE models (Song et al., 2021b) provide numerically accurate log-likelihoods via the probability flow ODE.

Feature-space methods.

A complementary family of methods detects OOD samples by their position in the feature space of a pretrained or jointly trained network, without fitting an explicit density. Lee et al. (2018) use the Mahalanobis distance to class-conditional Gaussian fits in feature space. Liu et al. (2020) exploit the energy function implicit in classifier logits. Sun et al. (2022) show that kk-NN distance in the penultimate feature space outperforms many parametric alternatives. These methods depend on a single representation space; combining multiple encoders requires an explicit fusion strategy.

Multi-encoder and ensemble detection.

Ensemble and multi-view approaches to OOD detection are relatively unexplored. Shalev et al. (2018) show, in a text setting, that replacing a single label embedding with multiple dense semantic representations from different corpora or architectures improves OOD discrimination—an early demonstration that representation diversity across sources provides complementary detection signal. Prior works that combine multiple representation spaces in vision typically do so by concatenation or majority voting, without a theoretical account of when combination helps and when it is redundant.

Multiple hypothesis testing.

The minimum pp-value statistic for combining independent tests is classical: Tippett’s test rejects the global null when mink⁡pk<τ\min_{k}p_{k}<\tau, with τ\tau set to control the family-wise error rate (Westfall and Young, 1993). Fisher’s method (Westfall and Young, 1993) provides an alternative via −2∑klogpk∼χ22​K-2\sum_{k}\log p_{k}\sim\chi^{2}_{2K}, which is more powerful when multiple tests simultaneously reject; Tippett’s test (and our min⁡(⋅)\min(\cdot)-gate) is more powerful when a single test dominates. Given the encoder specialization we observe—each encoder covers a distinct shift type—Tippett’s approach is the natural choice: one encoder typically dominates for any given OOD shift type.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Representation Space and Notation

Let {E1,…,EK}\{E_{1},\ldots,E_{K}\} be a fixed set of pretrained image encoders, Ek:𝒳→ℝdkE_{k}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}. We use K=3K\!=\!3: CLIP ViT-B/32 (d1=512d_{1}\!=\!512), DINOv2 ViT-B/14 (d2=768d_{2}\!=\!768), and ResNet-50 penultimate layer (d3=2048d_{3}\!=\!2048). For each encoder we define n=2n=2 normalization forks:

zk,n\displaystyle z_{k,\mathrm{n}} =(Ek​(x)−μk)/σk,\displaystyle=(E_{k}(x)-\mu_{k})/\sigma_{k}, zk,u\displaystyle z_{k,\mathrm{u}} =Ek​(x),\displaystyle=E_{k}(x),

where μk,σk\mu_{k},\sigma_{k} are per-dimension statistics estimated on the ID training set only. Normalization amplifies fine-grained structure within each encoder’s distribution; the unnormed fork retains the raw geometry.

Remark 1.

Within each encoder, the normed fork is more sensitive to covariate shifts and the unnormed fork holds a marginal edge on semantic OOD—a consequence of per-dimension Z-score normalization expanding the dynamic range of score differences under perturbations.

3.2 Score Network Architecture and Per-Encoder Density Models

Per-encoder models.

For each fork (k,f)(k,f) we train an independent VP-SDE score network (Song et al., 2021b) with linear noise schedule β⁡(t)=βmin+t⁡(βmax−βmin)\beta(t)=\beta_{\mathrm{min}}+t(\beta_{\mathrm{max}}-\beta_{\mathrm{min}}), βmin=0.1\beta_{\mathrm{min}}=0.1, βmax=20\beta_{\mathrm{max}}=20. The score network is an MLP with hidden dimension Hk=2​dkH_{k}=2d_{k} and depth L=6L=6 residual layers—capacity proportional to the encoder’s intrinsic complexity. All models are trained with Adam (Song et al., 2021b, lr=×10−42\!\times\!10^{-4}, up to 500 epochs with early stopping), batch size 512, gradient clipping (max norm 1.0). The probability flow ODE (PF-ODE) corresponding to the VP-SDE provides an exact log-likelihood via the instantaneous change-of-variables formula and Hutchinson trace estimation with MM random probes:

ℓk,f​(z)≜log⁡pθ(k,f)​(z)=log⁡pT​(z~)−∫0T∇⋅fθ​(z~​(t),t)​𝑑t,\ell_{k,f}(z)\triangleq\log p_{\theta}^{(k,f)}(z)=\log p_{T}(\tilde{z})-\int_{0}^{T}\nabla\cdot f_{\theta}(\tilde{z}(t),t)\,dt, (1)

where fθf_{\theta} is the PF-ODE drift and pTp_{T} is the terminal Gaussian prior. We use M=10M\!=\!10 Rademacher probe vectors and an adaptive ODE solver with relative and absolute tolerances of 10−510^{-5}. Let F^k,f\hat{F}_{k,f} be the empirical CDF of {ℓk,f​(zi)}\{\ell_{k,f}(z_{i})\} over ID validation samples. The transformed score

rk,f​(z)=F^k,f​(ℓk,f​(z))r_{k,f}(z)=\hat{F}_{k,f}\!\left(\ell_{k,f}(z)\right) (2)

is a pp-value: rk,f​(z)≈Uniform⁡(0,1)r_{k,f}(z)\approx\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1) for ID samples by the probability integral transform; small values indicate OOD.

Why monolithic concatenated models underperform.

A single score network trained on the full concatenated representation z=[z1;…;zK]∈ℝDz=[z_{1};\ldots;z_{K}]\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{D}, D=∑kdkD\!=\!\sum_{k}d_{k}, must enforce block-diagonal coupling in order to preserve the individual geometry of each encoder’s representation space: cross-encoder weight sharing conflates the distinct distributional structures of different encoders. Under this constraint, the score-matching loss 𝔼⁡[‖sθ​(z+σ​ϵ,t)+ϵ/σ‖2]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|s_{\theta}(z{+}\sigma\epsilon,t)+\epsilon/\sigma\|^{2}\bigr] is minimized by a score that acts independently on each partition—the optimal score s∗​(zk,t)s^{*}(z_{k},t) in partition kk depends only on zkz_{k}—so the model converges to a product of per-encoder marginals log⁡pθ​(z)=∑klog⁡pk​(zk)\log p_{\theta}(z)=\sum_{k}\log p_{k}(z_{k}), equivalent to separate per-encoder models but at 2.3×2.3\times more parameters.

Monolithic baseline.

For comparison we train a monolithic score network on the full concatenated representation z∈ℝ3328z\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{3328}. It uses a block-diagonal MLP with three encoder-aligned blocks of hidden dimension Hk=4​dkH_{k}\!=\!4d_{k} (yielding block widths 20482048, 30723072, 81928192 for CLIP, DINOv2, and ResNet-50 respectively), a total hidden dimension of 13,31213{,}312, and L=6L\!=\!6 residual layers—trained with the same VP-SDE objective as the per-encoder models. As shown in Table 3, the Hk=2​dkH_{k}\!=\!2d_{k} model fails on three of four benchmarks (SVHN 0.799, CIFAR-100 0.617, CIFAR-10C 0.631); Hk=4​dkH_{k}\!=\!4d_{k} is the minimum scale at which the monolithic model reaches ≥0.90\geq\!0.90 AUROC across all shift types, ruling out the possibility that the cost gap is an artefact of an over-parameterised baseline.

Model capacities.

Table 1 compares parameter counts. The six per-encoder models total 285M parameters; the monolithic Score Network baseline totals 647M. Per-encoder training is also parallelizable and can target smaller GPU budgets.

4 Encoder Analysis and Combination Design

4.1 ID-Data Diagnostics: Characterising Test Power

Different near-OOD benchmarks present distinct pain points—global domain shift, fine-grained semantic shift, and covariate corruption— where prior methods most often fail, each demanding a different kind of encoder sensitivity. The following diagnostics surface these differences from ID data alone.

η2\eta^{2}: class-conditional F-test.

Group {ℓk,f​(zi)}\{\ell_{k,f}(z_{i})\} on the ID validation set by class label. The ANOVA effect size

ηk,f2=SSbetweenSStotal\eta^{2}_{k,f}=\frac{\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between}}}{\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{total}}} (3)

measures the fraction of log-likelihood variance explained by class identity. High η2\eta^{2} means the density model reflects fine-grained class structure, predicting high sensitivity to semantic OOD (e.g. CIFAR-100). Conversely, a low-η2\eta^{2} model has learned a broad ID density that is not overfit to class detail, predicting sensitivity to global domain shift (SVHN) where class distinctions are irrelevant. We find Spearman ρ=0.771\rho\!=\!0.771 between η2\eta^{2} and CIFAR-100 AUROC across all six per-encoder models.

Δ​μ\Delta\mu: synthetic corruption probe.

Apply a fixed synthetic corruption to clean ID test images (GaussianBlur, kernel 3, σ=1.0\sigma\!=\!1.0; additive noise σ=0.1\sigma\!=\!0.1) and compute:

Δ​μk,f=μclean−μcorrupt.\Delta\mu_{k,f}=\mu_{\mathrm{clean}}-\mu_{\mathrm{corrupt}}. (4)

All corrupted images are derived from ID data; no OOD dataset is consulted. Large Δ​μ\Delta\mu indicates corruption-sensitive features, predicting high power against covariate shift. We find Spearman ρ=1.0\rho=1.0 between Δ​μ\Delta\mu and CIFAR-10C AUROC. DINOv2 is designed for corruption invariance (Oquab et al., 2024): its Δ​μ≈87\Delta\mu\!\approx\!87 (vs. 4171 for ResNet) correctly predicts its CIFAR-10C AUROC of 0.568 vs. 0.981.

ρ\rho: cross-encoder correlation screening.

Spearman rank correlations between per-encoder log-likelihood vectors on the ID test set quantify redundancy. Within-encoder fork pairs (normed/unnormed) yield ρ≈0.92\rho\!\approx\!0.92: nearly redundant on ID data, but differing in OOD-space geometry (the normed fork amplifies corruption sensitivity; the unnormed fork preserves raw semantic geometry). Cross-encoder pairs yield ρ∈[0.17,0.39]\rho\!\in\![0.17,0.39]: genuinely complementary, justifying multi-encoder combination.

Remark 2.

The η2\eta^{2} and Δ​μ\Delta\mu diagnostics reveal a strict encoder specialisation: no single encoder dominates across all shift types simultaneously (Figure 1, Table 2). CLIP maximises global domain-shift detection but underperforms on covariate shift; DINOv2 leads on semantic OOD but is nearly blind to corruptions (Δ​μ≈87\Delta\mu\!\approx\!87 vs. 4171 for ResNet); ResNet-50 dominates CIFAR-10C but ranks last on SVHN and CIFAR-100.

Table 2 further adds the η2\eta^{2} under synthetic corruption (ηcorr2\eta^{2}_{\mathrm{corr}}). Under corruptions, DINOv2’s η2\eta^{2} halves (0.243→\to0.112): class structure dissolves because DINOv2 features are explicitly trained to be corruption-invariant. CLIP’s η2\eta^{2} is essentially stable (0.096→\to0.092), consistent with its known sensitivity to class-discriminative corruption patterns. ResNet’s η2\eta^{2} drops sharply (0.109→\to0.046) because low-level texture features—the most corruption-sensitive—are class-agnostic.

4.2 Two-Level min⁡(⋅)\min(\cdot)-gate Combination

Because the type of distribution shift is unknown at test time, any fixed weighting of encoder contributions—including a monolithic concatenated model—will underperform on at least one shift type. The combination must therefore be input-driven: deferring to whichever encoder raises the strongest alarm for a given test point, without committing to any encoder in advance.

Algorithm 1 implements Tippett’s minimum pp-value combination (Westfall and Young, 1993): declare OOD if any individual test rejects. By Proposition 1 below, e^k\hat{e}_{k} is approximately uniform on ID data, so s⁡(z)s(z) is well-calibrated for threshold setting.

4.3 Theoretical Justification

Proposition 1 (Re-calibration between levels).

Let U1,U2​∼i​i​d​Uniform​(0,1)U_{1},U_{2}\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1). Then M=min⁡(U1,U2)∼Beta⁡(1,2)M\!=\!\min(U_{1},U_{2})\sim\mathrm{Beta}(1,2) with 𝔼⁡[M]=13\mathbb{E}[M]\!=\!\tfrac{1}{3} and PDF fM​(m)=2​(1−m)f_{M}(m)\!=\!2(1-m). More generally, mink⁡Uk∼Beta⁡(1,K)\min_{k}U_{k}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(1,K). Applying the empirical CDF G^k\hat{G}_{k} of {ek​(zi)}i\{e_{k}(z_{i})\}_{i} (ID validation) re-maps eke_{k} to an approximately uniform distribution, restoring the uniformity assumption for the Level 2 combination.

Proposition 2 (Min-gate power inheritance).

Let U1,…,UKU_{1},\ldots,U_{K} be the CDF-transformed per-encoder scores produced by Algorithm 1, and let M=mink⁡UkM=\min_{k}U_{k}. For any OOD distribution qq and threshold τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1]:

Px∼q​(M<τ)≥maxk⁡Px∼q​(Uk<τ).P_{x\sim q}(M<\tau)\;\geq\;\max_{k}\;P_{x\sim q}(U_{k}<\tau).
Proof.

M≤UkM\leq U_{k} for all kk, so {M<τ}⊇{Uk<τ}\{M<\tau\}\supseteq\{U_{k}<\tau\} for every kk; taking probabilities gives the inequality. ∎

Remark 3.

Proposition 2 is unconditional: it requires no distributional assumptions on qq. The min-gate inherits the detection power of whichever constituent encoder is most discriminative for the OOD type at hand—without prior knowledge of which that will be. The only assumption in the full system is encoder independence under pIDp_{\mathrm{ID}}, needed for the Beta(1,K)(1,K) null in Proposition 1; the power guarantee holds regardless.

5 Main Results and Experiments

EncMin2L is our proposed two-level min⁡(⋅)\min(\cdot)-gate combination (§4.2): it aggregates per-encoder log-likelihood pp-values via within-encoder minimum (Level 1), re-CDF recalibration (Proposition 1), and cross-encoder Tippett minimum (Level 2), calibrated on ID validation data alone with no OOD labels at any stage. We evaluate EncMin2L against classifier-based, feature-space, and diffusion-based baselines in the following experimental setting.

5.1 Setup

ID datasets. We evaluate under two settings. CIFAR-10 (Krizhevsky et al., ): ×3232\!\times\!32 RGB, bicubic-upsampled to ×224224\!\times\!224 for encoding; 50K train, 10K test with 10% held out for validation. CIFAR-100 (Krizhevsky et al., ): same resolution, encoder preprocessing, and split protocol, with 100 classes.

OOD benchmarks. Under CIFAR-10 as ID: SVHN Netzer et al. (2011) (global domain shift), CIFAR-100 Krizhevsky et al. () (fine-grained semantic shift), CIFAR-10C (Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019) (covariate shift, 15 corruption types), DTD Cimpoi et al. (2014) (texture), and CelebA Liu et al. (2015) (face domain). Under CIFAR-100 as ID: CIFAR-10 (coarser-grained semantic shift), SVHN, DTD, and CelebA. CIFAR-10C is omitted from the CIFAR-100 setting as no matched corruption benchmark exists for CIFAR-100.

Metrics. AUROC (↑\uparrow) and FPR at 95% TPR (FPR@95, ↓\downarrow; in parentheses throughout). Higher AUROC and lower FPR indicate better detection.

Baselines. Per-encoder: each of the six single-encoder models (E1/E2/E3 ×\times normed/unnormed) as individual detectors. Monolithic: Score Network trained on the full D=3328D\!=\!3328 concatenated representation in normed, unnormed, and dual-fork configurations. Classifier-based: Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP) (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017), Mahalanobis distance (Lee et al., 2018), and energy score (Liu et al., 2020) applied to a ResNet-50 classifier trained on the respective ID dataset. Feature-space: kk-NN distance (Sun et al., 2022) (k=50k\!=\!50) in the representation space of each pretrained encoder.

5.2 Main Results

Table 3 reports results for all evaluated methods under CIFAR-10 as ID. EncMin2L achieves ≥0.94\geq\!0.94 AUROC on all four benchmarks simultaneously—a bar no individual encoder or monolithic baseline clears—outperforming the best monolithic competitor (dual-fork Score Network) by +0.024+0.024 on SVHN and +0.047+0.047 on CIFAR-100 while using ×2.3\!\times fewer parameters.

The encoder specialisation predicted by the §4.1 diagnostics is directly visible in Table 3. CLIP (E1) leads on global domain shift (SVHN 0.977) but underperforms where semantic class structure matters, consistent with its low η2\eta^{2}. DINOv2 (E2) leads on semantic OOD (CIFAR-100 0.964) yet collapses on covariate shift (CIFAR-10C 0.568), exactly as its near-zero Δ​μ\Delta\mu predicted. ResNet-50 (E3) inverts this: its large Δ​μ\Delta\mu flags it as the covariate specialist, and it peaks at CIFAR-10C 0.981 while trailing on SVHN and CIFAR-100. Because each encoder has a structural blind spot on at least one shift type, EncMin2L’s min⁡(⋅)\min(\cdot)-gate defers to whichever encoder raises the strongest alarm per test point—and its worst-case AUROC of 0.951 (SVHN) reflects that no shift type is left uncovered. DTD and CelebA are saturated across all our models (AUROC ≥0.999\geq\!0.999 on DTD; 1.0001.000 on CelebA with FPR 0.0000.000), reflecting the extreme perceptual distance of texture patches and face images from CIFAR-10 objects; we discuss both jointly in §5.3. The monolithic dual-fork score network is the strongest monolithic competitor, yet EncMin2L surpasses it on both SVHN and CIFAR-100.

Under CIFAR-100 as ID (Table 4), the diagnostics again correctly predict encoder roles: E2 (DINOv2) leads on CIFAR-10 as OOD (0.9230.923), benefiting from its high η2\eta^{2} when the ID manifold spans 100 classes and the shift is to coarser-grained objects; E1 (CLIP) retains its SVHN advantage (0.9030.903). EncMin2L does not achieve ≥0.94\geq\!0.94 on SVHN (0.8060.806): E2 and E3 both assign high likelihood to SVHN under the richer 100-class ID distribution, creating a per-encoder floor the min⁡(⋅)\min(\cdot)-gate cannot overcome. Monolithic models remain the weakest near-OOD detectors, extending the isotropic noise finding beyond CIFAR-10.

5.3 Comparison with Feature-Space and Prior Methods

Classifier-based methods use a supervised ResNet-50 trained on CIFAR-10. Mahalanobis distance matches or exceeds EncMin2L on SVHN (0.957) and CIFAR-10C (0.981): class-conditional Gaussian distances capture large-scale domain and covariate shift well when ID class structure is informative of the shift. On CIFAR-100, however, Mahalanobis collapses to 0.830—the 10-class covariance model is too coarse to separate 100 semantically adjacent categories, exactly the limitation the η2\eta^{2} framing exposes: a covariance model can only be as fine-grained as the label set it was trained with. MSP and energy score are weaker overall. None of the three achieves ≥0.94\geq\!0.94 simultaneously across all four benchmarks; EncMin2L closes this gap without using class labels at any stage.

Under CIFAR-100, classifier-based collapse on CelebA is far more severe: Mahalanobis drops to 0.2820.282 (from 0.7720.772 on CIFAR-10) and Energy to 0.4510.451. With 100 class-conditional Gaussians the covariance model becomes too fragmented to maintain a coherent face-vs-object boundary. On CIFAR-10 as OOD, Mahalanobis also collapses to 0.4830.483: classes shared between CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (vehicles, animals) lie geometrically near the ID means, making Mahalanobis distance unreliable precisely where ID and near-OOD share semantic overlap.

Feature-space kk-NN (kk=50) on the same pretrained features uses identical representations but replaces the learned density with a non-parametric distance score. Under CIFAR-10 as ID, DINOv2 kk-NN (E2) exceeds EncMin2L on SVHN (0.978 vs. 0.951) and CIFAR-100 (0.976 vs. 0.942), yet collapses on CIFAR-10C (0.867). The diagnostics explain this directly: DINOv2’s corruption-invariant features (Δ​μ=28\Delta\mu\!=\!28) render training neighbours nearly indistinguishable from corrupted images, so nearest-neighbour proximity is not a reliable covariate-shift signal. ResNet-50 kk-NN inverts the pattern—strong on SVHN (0.970) and CIFAR-10C (0.936) but poor on CIFAR-100 (0.775)—its large Δ​μ\Delta\mu conferring covariate sensitivity at the cost of fine-grained semantic discrimination. No single-encoder kk-NN achieves ≥0.94\geq\!0.94 on all four benchmarks.

Under CIFAR-100, DINOv2 kk-NN (E2) becomes the strongest single method on near-OOD benchmarks (CIFAR-10: 0.9300.930; SVHN: 0.8810.881). The same encoder that collapsed on covariate shift under CIFAR-10 leads on semantic near-OOD under CIFAR-100, confirming that encoder utility is shift-type-relative: E2’s high η2\eta^{2} is an asset when the ID space is semantically richer and the shift is to coarser-grained classes.

DTD and CelebA: saturation gap. All per-encoder models and EncMin2L achieve AUROC ≥0.999\geq\!0.999 on DTD and 1.0001.000 on CelebA (FPR 0.0000.000), as do CLIP and DINOv2 kk-NN. Classifier-based methods do not: MSP 0.8560.856, Energy 0.8090.809, Mahalanobis 0.7720.772—a supervised ResNet-50 trained on CIFAR-10 object classes does not reliably flag face images because they have no equivalent class boundary to cross. Pixel-space diffusion methods similarly fail to saturate: EigenScore 0.8730.873, DiffPath 0.8970.897, LMD 0.8340.834, DM Dual Threshold 0.6480.648 on CelebA; EigenScore 0.7560.756 and Projection Regret 0.9100.910 on DTD. Modelling the ID distribution in representation space, where face and texture images have no support, is what makes the gap disappear.

Under CIFAR-100, DTD remains fully saturated (≥0.992\geq\!0.992) for all our models. CelebA shows minor degradation for E2 (0.9470.947) and E3 (0.9830.983) normed forks—the 100-class ID manifold marginally reduces the support gap for face images. Classifier degradation on CelebA intensifies further: Mahalanobis reaches 0.2820.282, reinforcing that representation-space density modelling is insensitive to ID label granularity in a way class-boundary distances are not.

Head-to-head: Representation-space diffusion. Järve et al. (2025) independently apply the same core hypothesis on the same CIFAR-10 ID dataset, training a Variational Diffusion Model (VDM) on ResNet-18 penultimate features (512-d). EncMin2L outperforms their best likelihood-based score (VDM log pTp_{T}) by +0.012+0.012 on SVHN (0.951 vs. 0.939) and +0.057+0.057 on CIFAR-100 (0.942 vs. 0.885), consistent with encoder diversity: CLIP and DINOv2 capture semantic cues inaccessible to a single ResNet-18. They also report TKDL—a class-conditioned score requiring labels at inference—as their best single-encoder method, reaching 0.900 on SVHN. EncMin2L surpasses TKDL by +0.051+0.051 while remaining fully unsupervised, showing that multi-encoder combination recovers gains otherwise achievable only through supervision.

Under CIFAR-100 as ID, VDM degrades to 0.7770.777 on CIFAR-10 as OOD and 0.7550.755 on SVHN; EncMin2L maintains its advantage (+0.115+0.115, +0.051+0.051). A single ResNet-18 encoder lacks the semantic capacity to model a 100-class ID manifold, and the multi-encoder gap widens as ID complexity grows.

Remark 4.

Ding et al. (2025) independently apply a sub-VP SDE score model on a single pretrained encoder’s representation space at ImageNet scale, validating the same core hypothesis. Architecturally, this is equivalent to the single-encoder models in Table 3—a setting where EncMin2L consistently outperforms every individual encoder across all four benchmarks.

Remark 5.

Representation-space diffusion methods are architecturally closest to EncMin2L—the same PF-ODE log-likelihood, the same compressed representation space. Under CIFAR-10 ID, the gap is already explained by single-encoder scope. Under CIFAR-100, VDM’s steeper degradation confirms that multi-encoder coverage is the variable that scales with ID complexity, not the choice of diffusion formulation.

Head-to-head: Pixel-space diffusion. Heng et al. (2024) propose DiffPath, which extracts a 6-dimensional statistic from the score-function trajectory of a pixel-space DM and fits a GMM in that space. With CIFAR-10 as ID, a CelebA-trained model applied zero-shot yields AUROC 0.910 on SVHN, 0.590 on CIFAR-100, and 0.923 on DTD. EncMin2L outperforms on both: +0.041+0.041 on SVHN and +0.352+0.352 on CIFAR-100. The CIFAR-100 gap is particularly large: pixel-space trajectories capture global distribution shift but miss the fine-grained semantic structure that representation-space log-likelihoods encode—precisely the class-conditional variance that η2\eta^{2} (0.0960.096–0.2430.243) measures and that is absent in raw pixel trajectories. DiffPath’s zero-shot universality comes at the cost of ID-specific semantic sensitivity; EncMin2L trades universality for precise density modelling on the ID manifold.

Under CIFAR-100 as ID, DiffPath’s near-OOD performance collapses to 0.4830.483 on CIFAR-10 as OOD—near chance—while SVHN recovers to 0.7240.724. CelebA remains at 0.8870.887: face images present a coarse perceptual contrast that is relatively ID-distribution-agnostic. The pixel-space trajectory cannot resolve the coarser-grained/finer-grained class boundary that separates CIFAR-10 from a CIFAR-100 ID distribution.

Head-to-head: LL+LID dual-threshold diffusion. Kamkari et al. (2024) flag OOD if log-likelihood log⁡pθ​(𝐱)\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) or local intrinsic dimension (LID) falls below a threshold, targeting the paradox that low-dimensional OOD data can receive high density yet low probability mass. Under CIFAR-10 as ID, their best DM variant achieves AUROC 0.944 on SVHN and 0.560 on CIFAR-100; EncMin2L exceeds both by +0.007+0.007 and +0.382+0.382 respectively. The large CIFAR-100 gap—despite the principled LL+LID combination—confirms that pixel-space LID cannot substitute for the semantic class structure that representation-space log-likelihoods encode.

Under CIFAR-100 as ID, DM Dual Threshold’s SVHN AUROC rises to 0.9450.945, now exceeding EncMin2L (0.8060.806): the richer ID distribution sharpens the global domain gap for pixel-space LL. On CIFAR-10 as OOD it reaches only 0.7910.791 (−0.101-0.101 vs. EncMin2L’s 0.8920.892): near-OOD failure deepens as ID and OOD share an increasingly overlapping class taxonomy.

Head-to-head: Inpainting-based diffusion. Liu et al. (2023) propose LMD, which masks an image with a checkerboard pattern, reconstructs via DDPM inpainting, and scores OOD-ness by LPIPS perceptual distance. Under CIFAR-10 as ID, LMD reaches 0.992 on SVHN, surpassing EncMin2L (0.951): inpainting fails visibly on house-number images, making the perceptual gap large and discriminative. On CIFAR-100, LMD drops to 0.607 (−0.335-0.335 vs. EncMin2L’s 0.942): CIFAR-100 shares visual structure with CIFAR-10, so DDPM reconstruction succeeds and the perceptual score collapses—the class-conditional density structure (η2=0.096\eta^{2}=0.096–0.2430.243) that drives our detection is invisible to pixel reconstruction.

Under CIFAR-100 as ID, the asymmetry intensifies: LMD reaches 0.9850.985 on SVHN (exceeding EncMin2L’s 0.8060.806) but collapses to 0.5680.568 on CIFAR-10 as OOD. Reconstruction succeeds precisely when visual structure is shared between ID and OOD, and CIFAR-10’s semantic overlap with CIFAR-100 is near-maximal.

Head-to-head: Projection-based diffusion. Choi et al. (2023) propose Projection Regret (PR), scoring OOD-ness by the LPIPS distance between a test image and its diffusion-based projection, with recursive projections to cancel background statistics. Under CIFAR-10 as ID, PR achieves AUROC 0.993 on SVHN, exceeding EncMin2L by +0.042+0.042: perceptual distance is highly discriminative when global domain statistics differ sharply. On CIFAR-100, however, PR drops to 0.775 (−0.167-0.167 vs. EncMin2L’s 0.942): CIFAR-100 shares background statistics with CIFAR-10, so the projection reconstructs OOD images convincingly and the score collapses precisely where η2\eta^{2} is highest. EncMin2L sacrifices only −0.042-0.042 on SVHN for AUROC≥0.94\geq\!0.94 across all benchmarks— balancing semantic sensitivity for global-shift detection.

Under CIFAR-100 as ID, Projection Regret reaches 0.9450.945 on SVHN (vs. EncMin2L’s 0.8060.806) but drops to 0.5770.577 on CIFAR-10 as OOD and 0.9100.910 on DTD (vs. our 1.0001.000). Background-statistics cancellation is effective when the global domain gap is large; it provides no signal when ID and OOD share the same object taxonomy.

Head-to-head: Posterior-covariance diffusion. Shoushtari et al. (2026) propose EigenScore, which uses the eigenvalue spectrum of a diffusion denoiser’s posterior covariance as the OOD signal: OOD inputs inflate the leading eigenvalues, yielding a Jacobian-free spectral detector. Under CIFAR-10 as ID, EigenScore achieves AUROC 0.810 on SVHN and 0.880 on CIFAR-100; EncMin2L outperforms on both by +0.141+0.141 and +0.062+0.062 respectively. EigenScore’s CIFAR-100 result (0.880) is the strongest among all pixel-space diffusion methods surveyed, suggesting posterior covariance partially recovers semantic structure—yet the residual −0.062-0.062 gap reflects class-conditional density geometry that η2\eta^{2} (0.0960.096–0.2430.243) quantifies and that pixel-space denoisers cannot fully access.

Under CIFAR-100 as ID, EigenScore deteriorates across all four benchmarks: CIFAR-10 0.6420.642, SVHN 0.6610.661, DTD 0.6270.627, CelebA 0.4270.427. Even DTD and CelebA lose the separation gap: a richer 100-class ID distribution inflates the posterior covariance baseline, reducing spectral contrast for all OOD types.

Remark 6.

Across all pixel-space diffusion methods—trajectory (DiffPath), inpainting (LMD), projection (PR), LL+LID dual-threshold, and posterior covariance (EigenScore)—a consistent asymmetry holds under both ID settings: strong on SVHN (global domain shift), weak on semantic near-OOD. Under CIFAR-100 as ID, three methods (DM Dual Threshold, LMD, Projection Regret) exceed EncMin2L on SVHN (0.9450.945/0.9850.985/0.9450.945 vs. 0.8060.806), yet all three collapse on CIFAR-10 as OOD (0.4830.483–0.7910.791). Pixel-space representations cannot access the class-conditional density geometry (η2=0.096\eta^{2}\!=\!0.096–0.2430.243) that drives semantic discrimination in representation space.

5.4 Encoder Contribution: Leave-One-Out Ablation

Table 5 reports EncMin2L with each encoder removed in turn on the three near-OOD benchmarks; DTD and CelebA are omitted as all configurations saturate at ≥0.999\geq\!0.999. Each drop directly confirms the specialisation the §4.1 diagnostics predicted from ID data alone.

Removing E1 (CLIP) cuts SVHN AUROC by −0.122-0.122 while leaving CIFAR-100 and CIFAR-10C stable: CLIP’s low η2\eta^{2} marks it as the global-domain-shift specialist, with little contribution elsewhere.

Removing E2 (DINOv2) drops CIFAR-100 AUROC by −0.113-0.113; SVHN and CIFAR-10C improve slightly, a complementarity effect explained by E2’s near-zero Δ​μ\Delta\mu—its corruption-invariant features were a drag on covariate-shift benchmarks. DINOv2’s high η2=0.243\eta^{2}\!=\!0.243 identified this semantic specialisation before any OOD data were observed.

Removing E3 (ResNet-50) causes the largest single drop: CIFAR-10C falls by −0.127-0.127, while SVHN and CIFAR-100 improve slightly, confirming that E3’s large Δ​μ\Delta\mu makes it indispensable for covariate shift.

6 Discussion

Encoder Generalization Advantage.

The diagnostic pipeline applies to any pretrained encoder: compute η2\eta^{2} and Δ​μ\Delta\mu on ID data, screen for complementary pairs via Spearman ρ\rho, then train per-encoder diffusion models only for encoders that add coverage. A natural screening criterion is ρ<0.5\rho<0.5 between the candidate encoder and all currently selected encoders; the remaining encoders each bring genuinely new information. This makes the framework a practical design-time tool for multi-encoder OOD detector construction without ever needing OOD examples.

Recalibration-free Detection Advantage.

The joint threshold τ\tau is calibrated at FPR α=0.05\alpha\!=\!0.05 on the ID validation set. Because the combined score s⁡(z)s(z) is approximately uniform on ID data (Proposition 1), changing α\alpha amounts to a direct rescaling of τ\tau: the empirical FPR at any other α′\alpha^{\prime} can be read directly from the ID validation CDF without recalibration. This makes the system straightforwardly adjustable for deployment scenarios with different false-positive budgets (e.g. conservative α=0.01\alpha\!=\!0.01 for safety-critical applications vs. permissive α=0.10\alpha\!=\!0.10 for screening).

Limitations.

The synthetic corruption probe (Δ​μ\Delta\mu) uses a fixed two-stage perturbation (Gaussian blur + additive noise) to approximate covariate shift. While this correctly ranks encoder sensitivity in our experiments, it may not generalize to all covariate shift types (e.g. weather effects, sensor noise). Users should run the probe with domain-relevant corruptions when the expected shift type is known. The min⁡(⋅)\min(\cdot)-gate’s formal hypothesis testing guarantee (Tippett’s test) requires the per-encoder pp-values to be independent under H0H_{0}. In practice, Spearman correlations of 0.17–0.39 between encoder pairs indicate moderate dependence. Near-OOD cases where OOD distribution partially overlaps with ID distribution (e.g. CIFAR-10 “truck” vs. CIFAR-100 “truck” classes) remain challenging for all density-based methods.

7 Conclusion

We presented a framework that statistically identifies the strengths and weaknesses of pretrained encoders from ID data alone, and introduces EncMin2L—an encoder-agnostic two-level min⁡(⋅)\min(\cdot)-gate for combining and calibrating per-encoder diffusion-based likelihood OOD detectors—achieving ≥0.94\geq\!0.94 AUROC across all four shift types simultaneously and outperforming the state-of-the-art diffusion OOD detectors at ×2.3\!\times lower parameter cost. η2\eta^{2} and Δ​μ\Delta\mu rank CIFAR-100 and CIFAR-10C AUROCs with Spearman ρ=0.771\rho\!=\!0.771 and ρ=1.0\rho\!=\!1.0 respectively before any OOD examples are observed, and leave-one-out ablations confirm that each encoder contributes precisely where its diagnostic profile predicted.
